albums.source: A live set I could not stop thinking about
albums.take: Recorded live and it *sounds* like it, in the way that is a compliment.
albums.review:
A friend put me on to this after a live set she could not stop talking about, and I went in expecting to be told the room was the point. The room is the point. It is also not the whole of it.

The band recorded four nights in one hall and kept the takes with the mistakes in them. You can hear a chair go over somewhere in the second track and nobody stops. The sleeve says it plainly:

> Four nights, one hall, everything kept.

**That decision is the record**: it is a document of four evenings rather than a performance assembled afterwards out of the best halves of each.

*Large Rooms* is where [a live record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_album) pays off. Seven minutes, one idea, and a piano that keeps finding a way further into it. I have played it more than anything else this month and I still do not know where the turn at four minutes comes from.

The rest is patchier than I want it to be. Two things drag it:

- Small Hours opens the record on its slowest idea and asks a lot of a listener who has not been given a reason yet
- two of the middle tracks are the same shape as each other, and the second one loses

None of that is a complaint about the playing. It is a complaint about the running order, which is a fixable thing, and which nobody fixed.

Keeping it, on [the shelf](/vinyl) next to [the kitchen record](/dan-fm/2026-08-26-cassette-sunday-two-weeks-in-the-hills). The back half earns the front half, and a record with one seven-minute track I will never get tired of is worth more to me than a tidier one I would put on less.

albums.take: Immaculate production doing a lot of work for songs that are mostly fine.
The best thing I have heard all month and it was recorded in somebody's kitchen.
albums.review: Nine songs, no studio, and not one of them outstays its welcome. The kitchen is the *whole* charm.

albums.source: A zine I found in a box

albums.take: Four songs in I stopped doing anything else. Track seven is the one I keep going back for.
albums.review:
Heard it on the radio driving home and pulled over to find out what it was, which has happened maybe four times in my life.

Anyone Else is the one. The whole record is one voice and not much else, and for four songs that is exactly enough - then Postcard arrives with a string arrangement it does not need and the spell breaks for a couple of minutes.

Came back to it a fortnight later and liked it less than I did the first night, which is the reading I have recorded as the later score. Some of that first four and a half was the drive and the dark and the surprise.

albums.take: Forty minutes of a band shouting "we are not for you", which I believe, and yet here we are.
